question.problem:
Calls to a customer service center occur continuously in time, independently, and at a constant average rate of one call every $10$ minutes. If no calls have been received for $20$ minutes, what is the probability that the next call will come within the next $5$ minutes? Round your final answer to **three decimal places.**

current_example.problem: A malfunctioning internet server approves connection requests continuously in time, independently, and at a constant average rate of $2$ requests per minute. If a user has been waiting for $30$ seconds to connect, what is the probability that they will have to wait at least $20$ more seconds?
current_example.worked_solution:
Since connection request approval occurs continuously, independently, and at a constant average rate, we can model the time until the next request is approved using an exponential distribution.

Let $X$ be the user's waiting time in seconds. Since the server approves $2$ requests per minute on average (or $1$ request every $30$ seconds), the rate is $\lambda = \dfrac{1}{30}$ requests per second, and we can write

$$
X\sim \textrm{Exp} \left( \dfrac{1}{30} \right).
$$

Recall that exponential random variables have the memoryless property. So, given two positive real numbers $s, t,$ we have that

$$
P(X>s+t \, \big|\, X>s) = P(X > t) = e^{-\lambda t}.
$$

In our case, we have $\lambda = \dfrac{1}{30},$ $s=30,$ and $t=20.$ 

Substituting these values into the above formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>30+20\,|\,X>30) & =P(X>20) \\  & ={e}^{-\lambda t} \\  & ={e}^{-(1/30)\cdot (20)} \\  & ={e}^{-2/3} \\  & ≈0.513.\end{aligned}
$$
